analysis.one_liner: Permanently eliminates the federal estate tax on large inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax, which applies only to the largest estates left after someone dies, and it would also keep 'stepped-up basis,' a rule that lets heirs avoid capital gains tax on any growth in the value of inherited assets. Together, that means the largest inherited fortunes would pass to heirs completely untaxed. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates — families with many millions of dollars in stocks, businesses, or real estate. The estate tax already exempts the first several million dollars of an estate (more for married couples), so repeal would help only the top fraction of one percent of inheritances, and the largest ones most.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal estate tax (chapter 11 of the Internal Revenue Code) for estates of people dying after December 31, 2020.

Retains stepped-up basis at death, so heirs would pay no estate tax and also no capital gains tax on the growth in value of inherited assets over the deceased owner's lifetime — a complete pass for the largest inheritances.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury, and therefore all other federal taxpayers, who would have to make up the lost revenue through borrowing, spending cuts, or other taxes.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the estate tax would permanently remove tens of billions of dollars a year in federal revenue, a cost shifted to other taxpayers or to federal borrowing.

Because the tax only applies to estates above a multi-million-dollar exemption, the bill's benefit would go almost entirely to a tiny share of the largest inheritances; the exemption already protects the vast majority of families.

Keeping stepped-up basis alongside repeal would mean wealth accumulated over a lifetime would never face income tax or estate tax at transfer, deepening the untaxed intergenerational transfer of large fortunes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes to a very small, very wealthy group; the cost is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes. Almost all families were already exempt from the estate tax, so the bill is nearly pure gain for large estates and pure revenue loss for the Treasury. Even sympathetic arguments about family farms and small businesses are largely addressed by the existing exemption, which the bill does nothing to scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never scheduled it for a vote, so it quietly expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta (R-OH) introduced the bill on February 4, 2021, joined by Reps. Long and Gibbs.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Four Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
No committee markup, no vote, and no floor action ever followed; the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal taxpayers and the Treasury, which kept the estate tax revenue that repeal would have erased. Heirs of the largest estates missed the windfall the bill would have handed them.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the estate tax repeal bill on February 4, 2021.

for.name: 4 Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee vote in the full two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Republican — four cosponsors, no Democrats — and the Democratic-run Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates (top fraction of one percent of inheritances)
industries.note: The bill would have let multi-million-dollar estates pass to heirs free of both estate and capital gains tax; its failure means that tax obligation stays in place. Their interest ran directly against the Treasury and general taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth management services
industries.note: Firms that help large estates minimize estate tax exposure would have kept less work if the tax disappeared; the tax's survival preserves their market. Their interest is peripheral to ordinary people.

industries.industry: U.S. Treasury and general federal taxpayers
industries.note: Had the bill passed, taxpayers as a whole would have lost tens of billions in annual revenue, a cost pushed onto everyone else through borrowing or other taxes. The bill's death preserved that revenue.
